subject: chemistry
question_text: How does diborane react with CO?

mark_split.label: Why diborane reacts with a donor

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, IPE STUDY MATERIAL for Jr. Students — Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.102, chapter 8 p-BLOCK ELEMENTS : GROUP 13, SAQ question 26(a). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints no per-step allocation on any answer in this chapter. This book prints no exam-appearance years for this chapter, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. EQUATION CHECKED AND CORRECT: B₂H₆ + 2CO → 2BH₃·CO balances at 2 B, 6 H, 2 C and 2 O on each side. CONDITIONS NOT ASSERTED: the prescribed book prints 1000 °C and 2 atmospheres, and this card deliberately does NOT print those numbers. Standard reference works give roughly 100 °C and about 20 atmospheres for borane carbonyl, and diborane decomposes well below 1000 °C, so the printed pair looks like a shifted digit rather than a measured condition. The card therefore says only that the reaction needs heating under pressure, which is true on either reading, and leaves the exact figures to a Telangana IPE teacher. The equation and the product name are unaffected either way.

steps.label: Why diborane reacts with a donor
lines: Diborane is electron deficient: it has 12
valence electrons where eight ordinary
bonds would need 16.
In its addition reactions the two bridge
bonds open and the molecule supplies two
BH₃ units.
Boron in BH₃ has only six electrons and an
empty orbital.
Carbon monoxide has a lone pair on carbon,
so it acts as the donor.
steps.why: Every addition reaction of diborane with a donor follows this one pattern: the bridges open, two BH₃ units are released, and each takes one lone pair. Writing the pattern once explains the reaction with carbon monoxide and the reaction with amines at the same time.
common_mistakes: Writing that the terminal B–H bonds break. It is the two bridge bonds that open.
Saying carbon monoxide donates through its oxygen atom. The lone pair used is the one on carbon.
steps.memory_tip: The bridges open, two BH₃ units form, and each takes one lone pair.
steps.margin_note: One sentence on the electron deficiency sets up the equation. Write it before the equation.

steps.label: The equation
lines: Diborane is heated with carbon monoxide
under pressure:
Atoms: 2 B, 6 H, 2 C and 2 O on each
side.
steps.why: One molecule of diborane gives two BH₃ units, so two molecules of carbon monoxide are taken up and two molecules of the product are formed. Checking the four atom counts is the quickest way to confirm the coefficients 1, 2 and 2.
common_mistakes: Writing B₂H₆ + CO → B₂H₆·CO. Two molecules of carbon monoxide react and two separate adducts are formed.
Leaving the conditions out. The reaction is carried out hot and under pressure.
steps.memory_tip: One diborane and two carbon monoxide give two borane carbonyl.
steps.margin_note: Write the conditions above the arrow, and check the atom counts before moving on.

steps.label: The product and its bonding
lines: The product BH₃·CO is called borane
carbonyl.
It is an addition compound, that is an
adduct.
Carbon monoxide donates its lone pair from
carbon into the empty orbital on boron.
The new bond is a coordinate bond, written
BH₃←CO or BH₃·CO.
Boron now has eight electrons and is sp³
hybridised.
steps.why: The product is not a new boron hydride; it is a BH₃ unit with a carbon monoxide molecule joined to it by a coordinate bond. The octet on boron is completed by the donated pair, and that is why the adduct is stable enough to be isolated.
common_mistakes: Drawing the new bond without showing where the pair came from. Both electrons come from carbon, so mark the bond with an arrow from carbon to boron, BH₃←CO, and the donation is visible on the page.
Writing the product as B₂H₆·CO. Each BH₃ unit takes one CO, so the product is BH₃·CO and two of them are formed.
steps.memory_tip: Borane carbonyl: one CO on each BH₃, joined by a coordinate bond.
steps.margin_note: Name the product borane carbonyl in words as well as in formula.

steps.label: The conclusion
lines: The product is borane carbonyl.
The reaction shows that diborane behaves
as two BH₃ units and that each unit is a
Lewis acid.
Trimethylamine reacts in the same pattern
and gives BH₃·N(CH₃)₃.
steps.why: The closing box carries the balanced equation and the product name in one place. The last line generalises the result: any molecule with a lone pair can open the bridges and attach to a BH₃ unit, which is the shape of this whole group of reactions.
common_mistakes: Writing one BH₃·CO instead of two. One diborane molecule gives two BH₃ units, so two adducts are formed.
Stopping at the equation without naming the product. Borane carbonyl is the name to write.
steps.memory_tip: Any donor with a lone pair opens the bridges and gives an adduct of BH₃.
steps.margin_note: Close with the balanced equation and the product name on one line.

insider_note: Diborane splits into two BH₃ units in this reaction, so the balanced equation needs two molecules of carbon monoxide and gives two molecules of borane carbonyl.
